name: PDRN / Polynucleotides

lead: PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide) is a mixture of DNA fragments, typically purified from salmon or trout sperm, used in injectable and topical skin booster treatments for rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after lasers or microneedling. It is widely used in Asian aesthetic clinics.

PDRN is proposed to act through adenosine receptor activation and by supplying nucleotides, supporting fibroblast activity, new blood vessels and calmer inflammation so skin repairs and texture improves. Polynucleotides (PN) are made of longer DNA chains and are described as acting mainly on matrix remodelling. The best-established clinical evidence concerns wound healing such as diabetic foot ulcers; a 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides in aesthetic medicine found nine studies covering 219 patients.

paras: It is usually given as a series of clinic treatments by small injections or applied topically after procedures, with products varying in source, molecule size and technique. Skin quality changes are typically judged over weeks to months.
Injection can cause bruising, infection and allergy, particularly to fish-derived material. Regulatory status varies, and many cosmetic products are not approved as drugs. Results differ by product.

angle.text: PDRN and polynucleotide skin boosters are injected or applied for skin rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after lasers or microneedling. DNA fragments support tissue repair, so skin quality and texture improve. Clinical studies exist for wound healing; cosmetic studies are smaller and vary by product.

lead: Polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN) is a mixture of DNA fragments, typically 50 to 1,500 kDa in size, purified from salmon or trout sperm and originally isolated from human placenta in Italy.[1][2] It is used in injectable and topical "skin booster" or biorevitalisation treatments marketed for skin rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after procedures such as laser or microneedling, and it is widely used in Asia as a dermatological biostimulator.[1][2][3]

People seek it out for smoother, more hydrated and more even-looking skin, for acne scar and post-surgical scar improvement, and for faster-looking recovery after resurfacing. Salmon DNA treatments have attracted interest on social media and in aesthetic clinics, and a 2026 dataset documents rising public search interest in PDRN and polynucleotides from 2019 to 2026.[4]

Related products labelled polynucleotides (PN) are made of longer DNA chains; a 2025 review distinguishes them from PDRN, describing PN as acting mainly on extracellular matrix remodelling and PDRN as acting through adenosine receptor activation and nucleotide supply.[5]

The best-established clinical evidence concerns wound healing, for example diabetic foot ulcers, rather than appearance. A 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides in aesthetic medicine identified nine studies of low to moderate quality covering 219 patients, with variation in injection techniques and products.[6][7]

paras: Wikipedia describes PDRN as a mixture of single-stranded oligonucleotides, peaking around 350 kDa in some commercial forms, obtained by fractionating and purifying DNA from salmon or trout sperm. A purification step is described as removing proteins and peptides that might trigger immune reactions, giving a product of about 95 percent purity.[1][2] The 2017 Frontiers in Pharmacology review describes a proprietary registered drug derived from Oncorhynchus mykiss or Oncorhynchus keta DNA, with a common molecular weight of 80 to 200 kDa and a peak near 132 kDa, and credits sperm-derived DNA with avoiding the protein, peptide and lipid contaminants found in somatic cells.[7]

Alternative sources, including plant, microbial and human-derived material, are an active research area, and lower-molecular-weight fragments are reported to penetrate skin and enter cells more readily.[1][2] A 2026 paper compared cordycepin-derived material with PDRN in a laboratory setting,[8] and another 2026 study reported effects of salmon-derived PDRN against skin photoaging in cells.[9]

In aesthetic clinics, PDRN and polynucleotides are injected into the skin in "skin booster" or "salmon DNA" treatments aimed at texture, hydration, fine lines, acne scars and post-procedure recovery.[3][6][10] Wikipedia reports that in Asia the most common application is as a dermatological biostimulator after abrasive procedures such as laser treatment or microneedling, mainly for purported anti-wrinkle and anti-ageing effects linked to collagen stimulation.[1]

A 2025 trial studied air-botulinum toxin combined with PDRN injections for acne scars.[11] A 2023 randomised trial examined early postoperative PDRN injections for hypertrophic scarring after thyroidectomy,[12] and a 2026 narrative review covers its use for recovery after aesthetic procedures.[10] Reviews of cosmeceutical use discuss extraction methods and topical applications.[2] A registered 2026 study of microneedling for skin health is also listed.[13]

PDRN has been used in wound care and musculoskeletal medicine. A randomised double-blind trial in Italy tested it on chronic diabetic foot ulcers,[14] a Korean randomised trial examined pressure ulcers,[15] and trials have tested ultrasound-guided PDRN injection for rotator cuff tendinopathy and PDRN eye drops after photorefractive keratectomy.[16][17] ClinicalTrials.gov lists PDRN studies in diabetic ulcers, scleroderma, rotator cuff tears, epicondylitis, spinal stenosis and menopausal genitourinary symptoms.[18][19][20][21][22][23][24]

The Frontiers review summarises the best-known controlled trial: in an eight-week study of diabetic foot ulcers, 110 patients received PDRN and 106 received placebo; complete wound closure was reported in 37.3 percent versus 18.9 percent, and median epithelialised area was 82.2 versus 49.3 percent, while time to complete closure did not differ significantly.[7] The review also describes a small trial of PDRN with hyaluronic acid for venous ulcers and smaller studies in pressure ulcers, knee osteoarthritis, lichen sclerosus, plantar fasciitis and female pattern hair loss, and notes that several of its authors hold patents or received research support related to PDRN.[7]

For aesthetic skin use, the 2025 systematic review reported low to moderate quality evidence across nine studies, with variation in injection areas and techniques, concluding that quality was limited.[6] Evidence specific to acne scars and surgical scars comes from individual randomised trials.[11][12][25]

The 2025 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology systematic review (registered with PROSPERO, covering English-language studies from 2010 to 2024) reported that, across its nine studies, polynucleotide injections reduced wrinkles, improved skin texture and enhanced elasticity, with statistically significant results in several studies, that side effects were generally mild and transient, and that patient satisfaction was moderate to high. The authors concluded that polynucleotides show promise but that consensus on optimal use is limited and higher-quality studies are needed.[6]

A 2026 narrative review in Cureus on post-procedure recovery searched PubMed, Scopus and CENTRAL and reported that randomised trials, comparative cohorts and split-face trials suggest PDRN improves re-epithelialisation, redness, scarring and pigmentation after procedures. It also reported that short-term cosmetic results were non-inferior to a hyaluronic acid filler, with possibly greater biostimulatory stability. The authors listed few randomised trials in aesthetic cohorts, small samples, formulation variability and a lack of long-term follow-up as limitations, and concluded that PDRN may be a reasonable adjunct subject to individual assessment.[10]

For aesthetic skin use, a 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides identified nine studies of low to moderate quality (219 patients) and noted variation in injection areas and techniques.[6] A narrative review of salmon-DNA treatments for post-procedure recovery was published in 2026.[10]

Randomised trials exist for specific scar and wound uses. The 2025 air-botulinum toxin plus PDRN study for acne scars and the 2023 thyroidectomy scar trial are examples, and a phase 4 registered study examined PDRN in post-operative scars (22 participants).[11][12][25] A 2026 registered phase 2 study compares fractional CO2 laser with and without PDRN for facial scars (36 participants).[26]

In wound healing, a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in two Italian centres evaluated PDRN for hard-to-heal diabetic foot ulcers, with a 215-participant study registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.[14][18] Wikipedia reports that studies in diabetic foot ulcers showed reduced healing time versus placebo.[1] Other registered trials include a phase 4 rotator cuff regeneration study (79 participants), an epidural PDRN study (45 participants) and a vaginal biorevitalisation study (136 participants).[20][21][22]

The most commonly proposed mechanism is activation of adenosine A2A receptors after enzymatic degradation of the polymer to adenosine, raising cAMP and upregulating pathways such as PI3K/Akt and vascular endothelial growth factor, with additional supply of nucleotides to the salvage pathway.[1][7][2] Reviews describe anti-inflammatory effects through reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines and NF-kB signalling, and promotion of angiogenesis and collagen production.[1][2][5] The 2017 review reports that an A2A antagonist blocked PDRN effects in cell experiments, and that in rats the half-life is about 3 hours, with about 3.5 hours in healthy volunteers after intramuscular injection.[7]

Laboratory studies report PDRN effects on fibroblast senescence and on SIRT1 in skin-ageing models, and a 2008 study reported angiogenesis and wound healing in diabetic mice.[27][28][29] A 2025 review states that PN and PDRN differ in function because of polymer length.[5]

A 2024 review states that in vivo tests and clinical trials have found PDRN non-toxic.[2] The 2017 review cites toxicity studies in mice and rats with no organ toxicity, excellent tolerability over 56 days in the diabetic foot ulcer trial, and a five-year post-marketing surveillance of over 300,000 prescriptions described as showing an excellent safety profile.[7]

Injection carries general procedural risks such as bruising and infection, and because the material is fish-derived, allergy is a theoretical concern; reviews describe the purification process as aimed at reducing immunogenicity.[1][7] The systematic review of aesthetic polynucleotides noted the least side effects as a goal of the field but concluded evidence quality was limited.[6]

The 2026 recovery review described the adverse-event profile in published aesthetic studies as invariably positive, while the 2025 systematic review reported mild, transient side effects across its nine studies.[6][10] Both stress the small size of the studies behind these reports.

PDRN was originally isolated from human placenta for pharmaceutical use in Italy and is now sourced largely from salmon or trout.[1] Wikipedia states that its most common application in Asia is as a dermatological biostimulator after abrasive procedures.[1] A Google Trends dataset published in 2026 documents public search interest in PDRN and polynucleotides from 2019 to 2026.[4]

Within aesthetic medicine, polynucleotide and PDRN products are marketed as "skin boosters", injectable treatments aimed at hydration, texture and skin quality.[6] Salmon-DNA facials and injections drew press and social-media attention as an Asian-origin treatment, and the 2026 Google Trends dataset documents rising public search interest in PDRN and polynucleotides from 2019 to 2026.[4]

Researchers are exploring non-fish sources and related materials. A 2026 laboratory comparison tested cordycepin-derived material against PDRN, and a 2026 marine-drug paper reported salmon-derived PDRN effects against skin photoaging in cell models.[9][8] Reviewers of the field describe formulation variability between brands, with PN (longer chains) and PDRN (fragments) marketed under overlapping names.[5]

A 2017 review of the compound's clinical use notes that several of its authors hold patents or received research support related to PDRN, a point researchers raise when interpreting the clinical literature.[7]

lore.intro: PDRN and polynucleotide treatments are discussed mainly by clinics, aesthetic practitioners and in review articles, with consumer interest visible in search trends.[6][4]

claims.claim: Salmon DNA injections improve skin texture, hydration and fine lines.
PDRN speeds recovery and calms the skin after laser or microneedling.
PDRN improves acne and surgical scars.
PDRN is an established treatment for chronic wounds.
Salmon-derived material can be an allergen risk because it is fish-derived.
